title: Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026]
Title:Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents. Nevertheless, as users expect agents to complete long-horizon, end-to-end tasks, they increasingly need to conduct broad information gathering, perform browser actions, and revisit acquired evidence within a single trajectory. Yet our preliminary analyses reveal that existing access models struggle to meet these demands. They primarily support either information gathering or browser interaction, while combining their capabilities can involve substantial costs or performance trade-offs. To this end, we present Web\$hell, an interface that unifies web access under a single access model. Using a common schema defined by WebContract, WebCompiler compiles live webpages into addressable information and action objects. These objects are maintained in WebCache and handled through a shared set of operations, providing agents with consistent, operable, and persistent web access. Through extensive experiments across web search, web navigation, and deep research benchmarks, we show that Web\$hell achieves strong task performance at lower cost. Our results further indicate the importance of interface design for effective web access, with Web\$hell opening new possibilities for more capable and efficient LLM agents on the web.

report.summary: Researchers propose Web$hell, a unified interface that compiles live webpages into addressable objects so LLM agents can search, browse, and revisit evidence within a single trajectory.
report.background: LLM agents are increasingly expected to browse the open web autonomously. Three access paradigms have emerged: search-augmented agents that retrieve snippets and crawl pages, browser-based agents that drive real browsers through DOM or vision actions, and filesystem-style agents that treat retrieved content as files for grep-like inspection. Each is strong in one mode but weak in others: search agents gather broadly yet cannot click, log in, or fill forms, while browser agents act precisely but burn tokens on screenshots, suffer brittle selectors, and lose earlier findings as context grows. Long-horizon tasks such as deep research or booking workflows demand gathering, interacting, and revisiting evidence together. The paper argues this mismatch is fundamentally an interface design problem, and that prior fixes combining both modes incur heavy cost or accuracy trade-offs.
key_points: One model instead of three: Web$hell replaces the split between search, browser, and filesystem agents with a single access model, so an agent uses the same vocabulary of operations whether it is searching, navigating, or re-reading an earlier page.

WebContract, WebCompiler, WebCache: a shared schema defines what a page exposes; a compiler turns live pages into addressable information and action objects; a cache keeps them persistent so agents can revisit evidence without re-fetching or re-rendering.

Persistent, addressable state: because objects keep stable addresses, agents can cite and re-open evidence mid-trajectory, avoiding the context loss and repeated scraping that inflate cost in long tasks.

Cheaper, competitive results: across web search, navigation, and deep research benchmarks the authors report strong task performance at lower cost than existing access models, suggesting interface design, not just model scale, drives agentic web efficiency.

Interface over model: the paper positions the interface layer as a first-class lever for agent capability, implying future gains may come from better abstractions rather than larger models or more tool calls.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Web$hell reframes agentic browsing as an infrastructure and interface problem, not merely a prompting or model-capability one. If the approach generalizes, agent platforms could standardize on a contract-style page representation, the way MCP standardized tool calling, letting competing agent frameworks share cached, addressable web state. For developers, the promise is fewer brittle DOM selectors, less screenshot-token overhead, and reusable evidence handles, which lowers the engineering cost of long-horizon research, shopping, or compliance agents. For regular users, the practical effect is agents that finish multi-step web tasks end to end, and citation trails you can audit, though it also raises fresh concerns about adversarial page content, caching of personal data, and sites losing control over how their pages are compiled and re-served.
report.tools: Follow browser-use and Stagehand for LLM-native browser control, Playwright and BrowserGym for automation and evaluation harnesses, WebArena and GAIA for agentic web benchmarks, and Firecrawl or Jina Reader for page-to-structured-text compilation. Anthropic's computer-use and OpenAI's Operator show the vision-driven alternative, while MCP and LangChain/LlamaIndex agent tooling are the natural integration points. Watch the Web$hell paper's code release and arXiv listing for the WebContract schema if you want to prototype compatible tooling.
